1:
Who Wisdom is decides how the chapter reads, and the disagreement opens at the first verse. Gill takes her for Christ outright, arguing from the subsistence with the Father, the eternal existence, and the personal properties ascribed to her throughout. Clarke refuses that sharply: wisdom is personified two ways only, as the power of judging rightly and as an attribute of God displayed in the works of creation, and has no other meaning in the whole chapter, whatever some of the fathers may have dreamed who find allegorical meanings everywhere. Wesley calls it a great question and will not settle it, since some passages agree better with the attribute and others with the person; possibly both are joined, and the chapter read of Christ partly in his person and partly in his office.

What they agree on is the contrast with the chapter before. Ellicott sets the secret allurements of vice under cover of night against the open invitation of wisdom, quoting the words about speaking openly and saying nothing in secret. Gill hears a herald lifting his voice at noonday in the public street, opposed to the whispers of a harlot at night in a corner: truth seeks no corner, and will bear the light. Henry reaches the same phrase independently: the adulterous woman spoke in secret and the heathen oracles muttered, but wisdom speaks openly, and truth seeks no corners but gladly appeals to the light. Clarke describes the transition as a waking: the wise man seems suddenly roused from contemplating young men ruined in both worlds by debauchery, by the voice of wisdom calling in the most public places.

Henry's reading is that revelation is easy to come at: proclaimed aloud, since wisdom cries and does not spare; from on high, the law given from the top of Sinai and expounded by Christ on a mount; and where the crowds are, the more the better. Clarke works the geography harder. The constituted house of the paths he suspects means the house of public worship, a centre to the villages around. But he will not leave it there: multitudes never enter such places, so wisdom must go out to them, which is why the zealous ministers of Christ still go to the highways and hedges, the mountains and plains, the ships and the cottages.

Delitzsch reads the scene as composition, not topography: the author heaps up synonyms which touch one another without coming together. He also defends the passage twice against Hitzig, who took the high places for a mountain summit and judged the second verse an interpolation, and rejected verses 4 to 12 as spurious. The high places are not summits, Delitzsch answers, and if this preamble is not to every taste it still belongs by its circle of conception and thought.

The address in verse 4 divides them again. Clarke takes the first word for men of wealth and power, the second for the whole race of Adam, so the call runs from the greatest to every individual. Ellicott makes the same distinction, comparing a verse of Isaiah where the two words are rendered great man and mean man. Gill will not have the distinction and reads men indefinitely, of whatever rank; Wesley says simply all men without exception. On the simple and the fools Delitzsch is precise — the first are those easily susceptible of good or bad according to the influence brought to bear, the second the intellectually heavy in whom the flesh burdens the mind — while Clarke turns the verse into a complaint about preaching. Preaching that is not pointed, that does not specify vices and charge them home on the conscience, never does much good; where the preacher assures his hearers that these were the crimes of Jews and Greeks but he hopes better things of them, he arms their consciences in double brass against his own teaching.
6:
The word rendered excellent things at verse 6 has been worked over hard, and Delitzsch reports the history. Hitzig understood it as things conspicuous; the Venice Greek as things set opposite; Kimchi as truths one makes an aim of on account of their worth. Fürst derived it from a root meaning to be elevated and therefore visible, so that the plural means principal or pre-eminent things — which is how the older versions took it, the Greek rendering solemn, Theodotion commanding, Jerome things of great matters. Delitzsch compares the law of love called royal, since it surpasses the other laws as kings do their subjects. Clarke arrives at the same sense by a shorter road, glossing the word as things pre-eminent and manifestly superior to all others, and adding the line that carries the point: the teaching is not trifling, though addressed to triflers. Gill hears princely things, becoming to him who is Prince of the kings of the earth. The second half of the verse Clarke takes as things calculated to correct false notions and set crooked ways straight.

Verses 7 and 8 are about the absence of a defect rather than the presence of a virtue, and the commentators work the negative words. Delitzsch notes that the verb behind the mouth's speaking signifies quiet inward meditation and, in poetry, the discourse coming out of it; that the contrary of truth here is wickedness in words and principles; and that the preposition before righteousness binds a quality to an action, so the sense is with rectitude, that is, truly. What is froward he defines as what has been violently bent and twisted, estranged from the truth and, so to speak, parodied. Clarke gives the same two words as tortuous or involved and as distorted, leading to obstinacy, and takes righteousness in the legal sense of giving each his due — what a man owes to God, to his neighbour and to himself. Ellicott's note is two words: froward means twisted or crooked. Gill turns the clause into doctrine, hearing the necessity of righteousness, the insufficiency of man's own, and the worth of Christ's.

Plainness is the claim of verse 9, and everyone qualifies it. Clarke renders the word straight forward, over against every man, level to every capacity, then makes the plainness conditional on self-knowledge: when a man gets the knowledge of himself he sees that all the threatenings of God are right, and when he obtains the knowledge of God in Christ he finds all the promises right. Ellicott makes the same condition scriptural, since the secret of the Lord is only with them that fear him and the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit. Wesley states it as the mind God has enlightened. Gill draws the sharpest form: the Bible is a sealed book to others, learned or unlearned alike, and the mysteries hidden in parables from them — though he adds that while some things in scripture are hard to be understood, those necessary to salvation are easy.

The last two verses set wisdom against money, and the difficulty is that the Hebrew appears to forbid silver outright. Delitzsch resolves it by a rule: such negations are understood comparatively, so the sense is not do without silver but acquire wisdom instead of it, and he cites an old Arabic saying built the same way — the fire, and not the disgrace. Clarke says the same in half a line: a Hebrew idiom for receiving instruction in preference to silver. Gill spells out the qualification: silver may be desired and received consistently with wisdom's instructions, and what is forbidden is the anxious and immoderate pursuit that hinders their reception; when the two compete, the one is to be preferred. On the last verse he collects the versions, which give precious stones generally, or pearls, or carbuncles, for what the English calls rubies.
12:
Wisdom now speaks in her own person, and Gill and Henry both take the speaker for Christ describing himself. Gill reads the first clause two ways at once — I inhabit prudence, the house I dwell in, and I dwell with prudence, my companion — and says either way it shows Christ fully possessed of it, as a man in a house is its proprietor. Henry makes it broader: wisdom here is Christ in the word and Christ in the heart, not only Christ revealed to us but Christ revealed in us. Ellicott gives the same verb without the theology, literally to have settled down and taken up an abode there — Delitzsch's rendering too, that wisdom inhabits prudence, is at home in its whole sphere and rules it.

What prudence is they define against something. Clarke calls it wisdom applied to practice, so that wherever true wisdom is it leads to action, accomplishing the best ends by the fittest means; and the witty inventions he renders knowledge and contrivance, the power of combining what is known of the nature of things to produce new results. Henry defines it against carnal policy, and claims more witty inventions have been found by the help of scripture — for understanding providences, countermining Satan's devices, doing good in one's generation — than were ever discovered by the learning of philosophers or the politics of statesmen. He then applies it to Christ, who found the costliest invention of all: we had found many inventions for our ruin, he one for our recovery. Ellicott and Wesley keep the plainer sense of well thought out plans and ingenious contrivances.

Verse 13 turns from what wisdom is to what she hates, and Delitzsch marks the structure: a new series begins here, and if the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, then wisdom personally considered stands toward God in a homage corresponding to that fear in man. Clarke draws the inference: it is impossible to hate evil without loving good, so hatred of evil leads a man to abandon the evil way while love of goodness leads him to do right, and the two together are the sum of true religion. Ellicott puts it as an impossibility of truce: there can be none between the kingdoms of light and darkness, so a friend of one must be the enemy of the other. Gill is careful which fear is meant: not fear of judgment and wrath, nor distrust of God's goodness, nor a hypocritical show of devotion, but a reverential and filial fear consistent with strong faith, great joy and true courage. Henry adds the application that costs something: everyone hates pride in others, but we must hate it in ourselves.

The last verses claim political authority, and Clarke counts the grades: five degrees of civil power are named — kings, consuls, princes, nobles, judges — and all orders of government are from God. He adds that many manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, with the Latin, read judges of righteousness rather than judges of the earth. Delitzsch works the words differently: the verb in verse 15 means not to legislate but to decree; the word for rulers comes from a root meaning to be weighty and so immovable, describing the repose that befits one invested with power; and the nobles of verse 16 are a fourth synonym for the exalted. Gill and Wesley agree on the qualification that matters. Kings are made kings by Christ and accountable to him, and the wisdom in their administrations is from him — but, as Wesley puts it, their injustice is their own, and only the good they do is owed to his conduct. Clarke says the same of counsel: a foolish man can give none, and the wise man only as he continually receives instruction from God.
17:
Delitzsch marks a fresh departure at verse 17: having said what she hates, Wisdom tells how she repays those who love her. Clarke traces the sequence by which that love arises. Wisdom shows itself, teaches a man the knowledge of himself, sets God's will before him, and makes plain the snares of life and the unsatisfactory nature of sinful pleasures; and if the heart then embraces that teaching and gives itself to God, his love is shed abroad in it by the Spirit — so we love God because he first loved us, and the more we love him the more of his love we feel. Ellicott sets beside the verse the promise that he who loves Christ will be loved in return. Wesley catches the tone of the first clause: I do not despise their love but kindly accept and recompense it. On the seeking early he is precise, taking it not of the hour but of the manner — with sincere affection and diligence, which is the evidence that the love is real.

Verses 18 and 19 promise riches, and the effort goes into qualifying which. Delitzsch works the adjective: the verb behind it means to move forwards, whence old, venerable for age, noble and unbound, and used of possessions it denotes goods that increase and endure. Clarke grants the plain sense first — the wise and discreet man often does arrive at literal riches and honour — then withdraws it, since this is not always so; what Solomon has in view must be the durable riches, the treasure deposited by God in earthen vessels. Ellicott allows that if the passage is taken materially one might compare the Pentateuch's promises of wealth for obedience, but holds the true riches are meant, the consciousness of God's favour, called elsewhere the unsearchable riches of Christ. Gill goes furthest, ruling out the riches of Christ's own person, which are not communicable, and temporal riches, which are not durable.

The fruit of verse 19 Gill takes as an image, wisdom being a tree of life whose fruit are the blessings of grace — redemption, pardon, justification, adoption, eternal life — and the graces of the Spirit besides. Ellicott reduces the two words to one gloss: the gain and profit that come from possessing her.

Verse 20 is about the road rather than the reward, and Delitzsch reads its grammar as a claim about constancy: the verb form expresses firm continual action, and in the midst means she turns aside from this line of conduct on no side. He also distinguishes the two ways the following infinitive can be taken, as the direction of the activity or its manner, and thinks both combine. Clarke's whole note is one sentence and the flat form of the same claim: nothing but the teaching that comes from God by his word and Spirit can lead a man in the way of righteousness. Ellicott supplies the parallels, a prayer for such guidance and a promise of it. Gill turns the leading into a doctrine of justification, since Christ leads his people off their own righteousness first, by showing it does not deserve the name and is insufficient to justify them before God.

What is inherited at the end is called substance, and Gill takes the word at its strongest. It renders what actually is, so the reality of the inheritance is asserted — not merely promised but already known, with the earnest of it in hand — and its solidity too, against the vain and shadowy things of this life. Delitzsch, looking ahead from the same verse, sees Wisdom taking another new departure, establishing her right to be heard and obeyed by unfolding what he calls her divine patent of nobility: she originates with God before all creatures, and is the object of his love and joy as he is of hers.
22:
Verse 22 is where the chapter became a battlefield, and every commentator knows it. Gill states the history: the Targum and the Greek render the verb created me, and it was that version Arius followed in concluding Christ a creature — the first creature God made, of a like but not the same nature, and the one by whom all others were made. Gill answers on three grounds. The Word of God is nowhere said to be created; if he were, God must have been without his Wisdom before making him; and Christ as the Word is himself the Creator of all things. He would rather render the verb begat me. Clarke reaches the same place another way. Wisdom is not acquired by the Divine Being — men and even angels learn it by slow degrees, but in God it is as eternally inherent as any other attribute — and the Targum and Syriac, by making wisdom a creature, are as absurd and heretical as some modern glosses on the passage.

Ellicott handles the verb philologically, not polemically. The Hebrew seems originally to have meant to set up or establish, and is used both of the forming of the heavens and the begetting of a son; only afterwards does it mean acquire, purchase, own. Since set up and brought forth follow as synonyms, the earliest sense is most likely intended, so Wisdom was formed or begotten before the creation — which agrees, he notes, with the Septuagint. Henry argues from the grammar of the whole passage: it is an intelligent and divine person speaking, not a mere property of the divine nature, because Wisdom is given personal properties and actions, and that person can be no other than the Son, to whom the principal things said here are attributed elsewhere. He concedes what the concession costs — Solomon may have designed only the praise of the attribute by which God made and governs the world — and answers that the Spirit who indited what he wrote carried him, as he often carried David, to expressions that could agree with no other than the Son.

The verb of verse 23 is unusual and nobody agrees on it. Gill takes it as ordained, following the Latin, or anointed, since anointing installed prophets and priests and kings, and insists the subject is a person and not a quality, a person and not a nature — the person of the Son, not the human nature, which did not yet exist. Clarke reads it as poured out or diffused, or from a cognate meaning to smear as with oil, so that some translate it I had the principality; and he concludes that all the schemes relative to creation were conceived in the divine mind from eternity, since there was no fortuitous creation, no jumbling concourse of atoms. Delitzsch rejects both anointed and the rendering woven or wrought that Hitzig and Ewald adopted, preferring Aquila's I was appointed. Wesley glosses it as constituted the person by whom the Father resolved to work.

Then the dating begins, done by subtraction. Delitzsch reads the depths not as primeval waters but as the inner waters, the treasures of the earth. On the settling of the mountains he asks the natural question — settled into what? — and answers with the Karaite Ahron ben Joseph that it is the bottom of the sea, since out of the waters they rise. Clarke renders the repeated verb I was produced as by labouring throes, and passes on Parkhurst's suggestion that the heathen poets took their Minerva born from the brain of Jupiter from some such personification. Gill takes both begetting and sequence as doctrine: this is the eternal generation and sonship, and to be before the mountains is a periphrasis of eternity used elsewhere of God, so its use here shows the Son's eternity the same as the Father's.
27:
The claim of these verses is presence at the work, and Delitzsch takes the first word carefully: the adverb usually means at that time, but here keeps its sense of place while including time — Wisdom was there when God created the world, having come into existence long before. Gill insists the presence was not a spectator's but a co-worker's, and Wesley says the same in three words. Clarke turns each clause into physics. No part of creation shows contrivance more than the visible heavens; the compass set upon the face of the deep he suspects refers to gravitation, since all particles tending to a common centre produce the orbicular form we see everywhere, so that even the waters take the circular figure in their aggregate of seas — the Hebrew being literally a sweeping of a circle. Ellicott takes the same phrase as the stretching of the vault of heaven, or else the circle of the horizon.

Clarke keeps the method up. The clouds above he renders the ethereal regions, the whole atmosphere with its meteors and vapours; the sea's decree he glosses as the assigning of its limits, the adjusting of its saltness, the proportioning of its surface to the vapour needed to water the land; and the foundations of the earth he takes for the irreversible laws governing its motions, the centrifugal force carrying it round the sun and the centripetal keeping its particles from flying off. Ellicott offers two corrections: established means made firm, and the strengthening of the fountains is more probably their flowing forth with strength. Wesley reads that clause the other way, of fountains shut up in the earth's cavities; Gill hears in the clouds waters bound up and yet not rent under the weight.

Verse 30 turns on a word nobody can settle. Clarke renders it a nursling, a darling child, and says Wisdom here represents itself as a new-born child ever near its parent, taking pleasure to see him act and to sport in his presence — all the images of the verse borrowed from a playful child. Then he issues a warning that runs against most of the other voices here: this is poetical and highly figurative, and those who think they find the deity of Christ in these metaphors should be cautious how they apply such terms, lest while endeavouring to defend the truth they do something against it — in which, he thinks, most unhappily fail. Ellicott allows the same sense — a foster child, as Esther was brought up by Mordecai — but prefers another, since the word may also mean artificer, which he calls much more suitable and better harmonised with the passages making Wisdom the agent of creation. Gill reports that two Greek translators rendered it strengthened. Delitzsch rejects two more attempts: Hofmann's continually, for which the word is not so used, and the Targum's believing or trusting, which he judges inadmissible.

Ellicott corrects one more thing: the pronoun in daily his delight is not in the Hebrew, which says literally I was delights, all joy. What that delight settled on the last verse says, and the readings converge. Delitzsch has Wisdom turning her love to the earth for man's sake, and to man not merely as a bodily but as a spiritual being, to whom she can disclose her heart and whom, if he receives her, she can bring back to God. Clarke says the delight that once rested on man's creation now rests on his instruction, so wisdom offers her lessons continually and uses every opportunity to call men from folly. Gill hears the ease of it: the word for rejoicing means sport or play, continuing the image of the nursed child. Wesley makes the delight the whole work of redemption: to uphold men, to reveal the Father's will to them from age to age, to assume their nature and save them.
32:
The closing appeal is a return, and Delitzsch marks it: having shown how worthy her fellowship is from her mediating place between God and the world, Wisdom begins the hortatory part of her discourse. He notes that the Greek omits verse 33 and removes the awkward and blessed of verse 32 by transposing the lines, though that conjunction is the beatitude's own. Henry states the purpose of the whole chapter from here: to bring us into subjection to the laws of religion and make us wise and good, not to fill our heads with speculations or our tongues with disputes, but to rectify what is amiss in our hearts and lives. Clarke reads the therefore back to the verse before: since I delight so much in conveying instruction, and have the happiness of the children of Adam so much at heart, hearken to me. Ellicott reads it the same way.

Waiting at the doors becomes a picture. Clarke has Wisdom keeping a school, her most forward scholars arriving before the gates open, to lose no accent of the teaching. Ellicott offers the same figure and two more, a courtier expecting his sovereign or a lover his mistress; Wesley makes it servants at the doors of princes. Delitzsch works the verb: it denotes not wakefulness after interrupted sleep but watching as a settled condition.

The last verse turns on missing rather than offending, and philology and theology agree. Delitzsch gives the verb its oldest sense, to miss something one runs after, seeks, or shoots at, and says the contrast with him that finds me puts it beyond doubt. Ellicott renders it he that misses me does not find me, adding that the Greek word for sin carries the same idea of missing life's true object. Gill fills in what missing means: looking for salvation elsewhere — by the light of nature, the law of Moses, moral performances, a bare profession. Clarke turns it on the man himself — it is not Satan, nor sin properly speaking, that hurts him, but himself, since if he received God's teaching sin would have no dominion and if he resisted the devil the devil would flee — and on loving death: a man who works for wages must love them, seeing he labours so hard.

Clarke then closes the chapter with a refusal of everything Gill and Henry have built on it. He has weighed every word, examined their radical import and their connection with what goes before and after, and cannot conscientiously reach another interpretation: the chapter speaks not one word about either the divine or the human nature of Christ, much less any eternal filiation of his divinity, and had there not been a preconceived creed no soul of man would have found the eternal sonship here by fair criticism. He knows the reading is ancient and does not care, since the fathers were not agreed — some taking the speaker for Christ, others for the Holy Spirit — and since there is not a truth in the most orthodox creed that cannot be proved from their authority, nor a heresy that cannot claim them. In doctrine their authority is with him nothing; the word of God alone contains his creed.

The refusal is not from outside. Clarke sets down what he does believe — the holy Trinity, three persons in the Godhead of which none is before or after another, Jesus in his divine nature as unoriginated and eternal as Jehovah — and says of the writers who prove the eternal sonship here that reading them has shocked him: they have taken away my Eternal Lord, and I know not where they have laid him. Neither side gives ground. Gill ends where he began, with finding Christ as finding life; Henry ends by telling the reader to read the word written, sit under the word preached, and bless God for both.
